resources.string: Runs a visible notification service that you start yourself. It checks which app is in front every 2 seconds while the screen is on, and does nothing while it is off. It does not start by itself after a reboot and draws nothing over other apps.
Needs \"Usage access\" so FrameX can see which app is in front.
When a selected game opens, its profile is applied; when you leave it, the previous settings are restored. Apps are never stopped automatically.
No games selected yet. Add some below.
No games detected. Turn on \"Show all apps\" to pick any app.
FPS unavailable: measuring other apps needs Shizuku or wireless debugging
Checks temperature, memory, battery saver and refresh rate, picks the profile, then starts the game.
Applies this game\'s saved profile, then starts the game. Automatic analysis is off in Settings.
The game was started without changes: FrameX needs Usage access to put settings back afterwards.
This app could not be started.
Battery saver is on. Android limits CPU and GPU in this mode, so FPS will be lower. Turn it off.
The screen is not at its highest refresh rate. Raise it in display settings if the game supports it.
The phone is hot. It will throttle and FPS will drop. Let it cool down, or play with the dimmed-screen profile chosen.
The phone is warm and charging. Charging adds heat; unplugging helps if it keeps heating.
Memory use is high. Stopping apps you choose may help.
Profile %1$s can stop background apps before the game. Tick the ones to stop. They may restart later and unsaved data in them can be lost. System apps are never listed.
Remember my choice for this game
FPS ESTIMATED from screen capture (about ±2): avg %1$s · min %2$s · 1%% low %3$s

No boost can make a game draw more frames than the game itself allows. FrameX removes system limits and lowers the cost of drawing, then shows the measured FPS with and without the boost so you can see what it really did.
No extra boost: only the profile from above is applied.
• Locks the screen to the highest refresh rate it supports (put back afterwards; skipped if the phone ignores it).
• Asks the system for fixed performance mode (where the phone supports it).
• Draws this game at %1$d%% resolution: less work for the graphics chip, a slightly softer picture.
These need shell access (Shizuku or wireless debugging in Settings). Without it only the profile above applies.
This game stops at about %1$d FPS by itself, so no boost goes beyond that.
Settings inside the game (only you can change them)
FPS with and without the boost
With boost: %1$s FPS avg (%2$d sessions) · without: %3$s FPS avg (%4$d sessions).
Play with the boost and with it Off, with FPS measurement available, to compare. Nothing is shown until there is real data for both.
Set the game\'s frame rate option to the highest it offers. No outside boost can lift a game above its own cap.
Turn on the game\'s high frame rate / 60 FPS mode in its settings.
Lower the graphics quality preset in the game.
Turn off shadows and effects such as anti-aliasing, bloom and motion blur.
Lower the render resolution or scale in the game.

Needs shell access. Turns on the Wi-Fi low-latency modes and Data Saver so other apps stop using your connection in the background, then puts everything back. It cannot make your internet line itself faster.

FrameX cannot generate frames itself: that is done only by the phone maker\'s driver or by the game. Some phones (usually pricier models) have a game booster (Game Turbo, Game Space, Game Booster) with options such as frame insertion or a higher frame rate. FrameX finds the screens that exist on this phone and opens them, but cannot see which features your model has. Turn one on, play, then compare the measured FPS in the game\'s card.
No game booster screens were found on this phone.
That screen could not be opened.
No special boost for this game

The tuned levels (Safe, Strong, Max) exist only for games FrameX has a strategy for: Brawl Stars, Clash Royale and Clash of Clans, Roblox, PUBG Mobile and BGMI, Call of Duty Mobile, Genshin Impact and Honkai Star Rail, Free Fire, Mobile Legends, Minecraft and Standoff 2. For any other game you can use Ultra, which does everything at once.

Strategy: this game is light on the graphics chip and stops at its own frame cap, so lowering resolution would only blur it. The boost fixes frame pacing instead: a screen rate that matches the game, and steady performance.
Strategy: this game is heavy for the graphics chip, so render resolution is the main lever. Max also dims the screen so the phone runs cooler.
Strategy: this game depends on both the processor and the graphics chip. The boost lowers resolution a little and keeps performance steady; draw distance inside the game matters most.
Strategy: steadiness and ping matter most here. The boost keeps performance steady, adds the Wi-Fi low-latency modes and lowers resolution only a little.
• Locks the screen to %1$d Hz, the rate that suits this game (put back afterwards; skipped if the phone ignores it).
• Adds the Wi-Fi low-latency modes (this game is ping-sensitive).
• No resolution cut: this game is not limited by the graphics chip, so it would only blur the picture.
• Max also dims the screen to about 30% so the phone runs cooler (needs the permission to change system settings).
• Lowers the whole screen resolution to %1$d%% while the game runs: the graphics chip draws far fewer pixels. Everything on screen looks softer meanwhile.
• No screen resolution cut: this game stops at its own frame cap and is not limited by the graphics chip, so it would only blur it.
• Data Saver: other apps cannot use your connection in the background.

Ultra changes the resolution of the whole phone while you play and puts it back afterwards, and it is set before the game opens, so start the game with the Play button. If FrameX is stopped meanwhile, it restores the resolution the next time it starts.
